headline: 7.4°F Split at 39°34' — Yellowfin Camped on the Warm Side of the Dip
subhead: A Gulf Stream filament pushed further north than it should for late July, and the canyon edge is holding fish because of it.
body_markdown:
Seven point four degrees. That's the spread I logged running the edge Tuesday between the shelf water sitting at 71.2 and the warm filament pushing into the Dip at just under 79. That's not a normal late-July number for this canyon — usually by now the whole shelf's evened out and you're hunting for a break instead of tripping over one. This year the Stream kicked a tongue of warm water north of where it usually sits, and it's been parked on the 100-fathom line for the better part of two weeks. That's the whole story right now. Find the color change where that warm water meets the green shelf water, and you find the fish.

I ran out of Manasquan Thursday, put the spread in at the Dip around 39°33'N/72°45'W, right where the canyon wall starts to break steep on the chart. Water there was reading high 70s on the surface, clean blue, with a hard rip line visible from a half mile out — you could see the foam and the weed collecting on it before you even got the lines wet. That's your visual cue. Birds were working it too, terns diving on bait pushed up against the seam. We picked up yellowfin in the 25-40 pound class on that edge, mostly on the troll — green machines and Joe Shute bars in the middle of the spread, naked ballyhoo with a chartreuse Sea Witch off the shotgun. Nothing giant, but a consistent pick, four fish in about ninety minutes of working that one temp break before it slid on us mid-afternoon.

The Claw was slower. I had a report of a bigeye taken there overnight on the chunk — butterfish soaked out on a fluorocarbon leader, no weight, dead-sticked back about sixty feet on the drift in 900 feet of water — but that's one fish, one boat, one night. Don't read that as the Claw lighting up wholesale. The warm water hasn't fully committed to that piece of structure yet; it's been more of a Dip and 100-fathom-line story this week, with the Claw riding the edge of the filament rather than sitting inside it.

Mahi have been the bonus fish, and an honest one — scattered, not stacked. We picked up a dozen keeper-class mahi in the 5-8 pound range working floating weed lines out past the Dip, mostly on small pink and white feather jigs cast ahead of the boat once we spotted the mat. That's a run-and-gun fishery right now, not a set-and-troll one. You need eyes on the water, not just rods in the spread. Some boats are finding bigger fish, 15-20 pounds, holding under isolated debris rather than the big weed mats — worth a look if you're marking floating junk on the way out.

Wahoo have shown up incidentally, a couple of cutoffs and one fish boated trolling a high-speed spread with a black/purple Braid Marauder at 14 knots along the edge of the warm water, which tells me there's a thermocline down there worth checking with the temp probe if you're rigged for it. White marlin have been quiet on my end this week — a couple of raises reported working ballyhoo dink baits south toward Wilmington, but nothing consistent enough on the Hudson itself to call it a pattern yet.

We flagged this last week — said the bite would hold as long as the weather pattern held, and that's exactly what's played out. Stable winds out of the southwest, light seas, and that warm filament refusing to slide off the canyon wall. The mahi call held too — scattered but consistent is precisely what we got, not a blitz, but reliable enough to fill a fish box if you put in the time on the weed lines.

Here's my read going into next week. As long as that 79-degree water holds its position on the Dip and doesn't retreat south, I'd keep working that same stretch — 39°32' to 39°36'N along the canyon wall, working the color change on the troll early, then switching to chunk and drift once you find bait stacked on the sounder. If you see the edge water start cooling back toward 74-75, that's your signal the filament is sliding off the canyon and you'll want to run further east toward Block or south toward the Elephant Trunk to find it again. Moon's building back toward the August 12 new moon, tides picking up incrementally through the week, which should help concentrate bait tighter to the structure rather than spreading it thin across open water. I wouldn't call this the best week of the summer, but it's a real bite on a real temp break, and right now that's more than a lot of boats can say. Watch the water, not the calendar.
